extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Emerson / readers interested in moral philosophy, character, and social manners
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-philosophical essay (Ralph Waldo Emerson) exploring the nature of moral character and social manners: what constitutes greatness of character, how it acts, and what manners/gentility truly mean. The text offers descriptive and prescriptive claims about personal qualities and social behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as a reserved force (presence over deeds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is 'a reserved force which acts directly by presence, and without means' — a latent power in some men by which their presence alone alters affairs and inspires reverence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples invoked: Lord Chatham, Mirabeau, Hercules — their reputation exceeds the record of deeds because their presence manifests authority. Such men often appear solitary; their victories are 'by demonstration of superiority' rather than by visible contests. This is contrasted with ordinary people whose reputation is tied to events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith in a fact / invincible persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: A public man must possess an 'invincible persuasion' of a fact in himself so that others perceive an impregnable resistance — this faith makes his talent trusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In political representation this quality is decisive: a learned, fluent speaker who lacks this internal conviction cannot carry points. The man with faith 'is himself the country which he represents' and needs not inquire of constituents what to say.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / nature, not imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is 'nature in the highest form' and 'best where no hands but nature's have been laid on it'; it cannot be successfully imitated or manufactured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: trying to ape character or adopting reform/virtues only by book-learning results in tentative, unconvincing action. Positive examples: children whose sanctity arises from 'nonconformity' and rural simplicity; the text warns that praise and publicity may spoil some natures but true character remains native.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnetism / power to influence others
rubrics_metrics.description: Great character includes a magnetic influence — a 'river of command' or 'torrent' from the person's eyes or presence that pervades others and compels obedience or inspires change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson offers vivid examples (Caesar in irons, Toussaint L'Ouverture) to show that moral presence can overcome physical constraints or social arrangements. This influence explains why some men can alter the behavior and thoughts of many without apparent force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sufficingness / centrality / sense of mass
rubrics_metrics.description: Character manifests as self-sufficingness: the person 'gives us a sense of mass' — centrality and the impossibility of being displaced or overset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with frivolous society and shallow conviviality; the gentleman stands 'stoutly in his place' and need not accept conventional opinions. This solidity provides refreshment and moral authority to observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral primacy: truth and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is 'the summit of being' and justice its application; character is the individual's embodiment of this moral order that naturally exerts influence on others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson argues the moral element in action preexists the act and runs from the person into others; even when appearances or isolated events suggest otherwise, 'justice must prevail' as a natural force linked to character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional action: act within one's substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions should 'rest mathematically on our substance' — one must not attempt undertakings beyond one's real capacity or force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipatterns: persons who strive for positions (e.g., Mr. Fox wanting the Treasury) without the requisite inner substance produce tentative, ineffective reforms. Positive precedent: Xenophon and his Ten Thousand succeeded because they were equal to their task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incessant growth / future-oriented character
rubrics_metrics.description: A trait of great character is continual growth: men should be intelligent and earnest and suggest 'a controlling happy future opening before them' — constantly adding new powers and honors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good men make new actions which 'are the only apologies and explanations of old ones'; a friend who has erred will soon 'double his power to serve you' by future deeds rather than explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benevolence measured by spirit, not enumerated works
rubrics_metrics.description: True charity and benevolence are inexhaustible qualities of the spirit and cannot be fully measured by a list of specific donations or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson criticizes attempting to quantify a man's goodness (Riemer's list of Goethe's donations) — the deepest evidence of charity is inferred from life and temperament, not from cataloged acts. Those who live to the future often appear selfish to present-focused observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonconformity as intellectual and moral stimulus
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal to accept conventional opinions and practices marks character and acts as a 'goad and remembrancer' to inquiry and reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonconformity preserves originality and keeps society from complacency; the 'uncivil, unavailable man' who challenges the establishment both irritates and benefits public life by breaking skepticism and triviality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of character requires time and perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Character 'wants room' and 'needs perspective' — it should not be judged hastily from few occasions or press-glimpses; full appreciation requires distance and duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson warns against rash popular ethics or premature biographies; great character may form relations slowly and be misunderstood if evaluated by immediate events or ephemeral press coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character's measure is resistance of circumstances; not event-driven
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural measure of character is how it resists circumstances; impure people 'consider life as it is reflected in opinions, events, and persons,' while true character remains prior to events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person's moral element can be predicted and does not depend on favorable outcomes. The hero sees events as ancillary — prosperity follows a certain mind rather than creating it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship and deep mutual understanding as supreme social good
rubrics_metrics.description: Profound reciprocal friendship between virtuous men — 'a profound good understanding' — is among life's most satisfying possessions and outweighs political, commercial, and religious satisfactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson elevates friendship (and love as its symbol) as the happiest relation: when two virtuous persons meet, it 'postpones all other gratifications' and makes public institutions comparatively cheap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners/Gentleman: truthfulness, independency, and benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: A gentleman is 'a man of truth, lord of his own actions, and expressing that lordship in his behavior' — not dependent or servile to persons, opinions, or possessions; gentility includes good-nature and benevolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson distinguishes genuine gentility from mere fashion: it is a compound of virtue, wit, beauty, wealth, and power; it signals personal force and benevolence rather than superficial polish or exclusive manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners: proportion, dignity, and the instructive effect on arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Outward manners and figure (proportion, color, dignity, reverence) instruct and elevate design and picture; the cultivated manners should sustain the arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted Ben Jonson lines advise composing oneself and 'putting aptness on / Of Figure, that Proportion Or Color can disclose' so that even if silent arts were lost, manners could provide a 'newer ground' for design and picture. Manners thus have educative and aesthetic dimensions.
